text: You've now got four separate pieces: what superposition really is, the Born rule, collapse, and basis choice. The only way to be sure they've stuck is to run them together on concrete problems.

Take psi equals root one-third ket-zero plus root two-thirds ket-one. Normalization checks out — one-third plus two-thirds is 1. The Born rule gives P of 0 about 0.333 and P of 1 about 0.667. Now add collapse: suppose this measurement yields 1. The state immediately becomes exactly ket-one — not retaining any trace of the original split. Measure again right away and you get 1 with certainty. Compute probabilities with the Born rule, then separately apply collapse for whichever outcome actually happened — that's the pattern you'll use constantly.

Lesson 11 showed Hadamard applied twice returns exactly ket-zero. Applying H twice with no measurement in between is fully reversible — H times H equals the identity, exactly. But if you instead measured the qubit while it was ket-plus, say getting outcome 0, you'd collapse it to exactly ket-zero, and that specific collapse is not reversible the way gate application is. Gates, unmeasured, preserve and transform superposition reversibly; measurement resolves it irreversibly. Confusing the two is one of the most common early mistakes.

Lesson 14 verified that ket-zero and ket-one, opposite extremes in the computational basis, produce identical 50/50 statistics in the X-basis. And lesson 12 showed ket-plus and ket-minus give identical 50/50 statistics in the computational basis, even though Hadamard treats them completely differently. Two complementary examples of the same fact: single-basis measurement statistics aren't a complete fingerprint of a state — a theme that becomes essential in chapter 4's Bell-inequality tests.
Chapter 4 moves to multi-qubit systems and entanglement — correlations between qubits that no single-qubit description, however you choose the basis, could ever produce.
